title: Kashmiri food: wazwan, nun chai and bakeries
meta_description: Kashmiri food explained: the wazwan feast, nun chai and kahwa, kandur bakeries, winter harissa, Pandit vegetarian dishes, saffron, and what each costs in Srinagar.
summary: Kashmiri food runs on mutton, rice, dried spices and milk-free gravies coloured with Kashmiri chilli and cockscomb flower. Learn the wazwan courses, start mornings with nun chai and bakery bread, try harissa in winter, and eat the vegetarian Pandit dishes too. Most plates cost ₹150–600 in Srinagar.

sections.heading: How Kashmiri food is different
paras: Kashmiri cooking grew out of a cold valley with short summers. Rice is the staple, grown in paddies across the valley floor. Mutton is the prized meat. Vegetables are dried in autumn for winter, and gravies are coloured deep red with mild Kashmiri chillies and, in some kitchens, the dried flower of the cockscomb plant, called mawal, rather than made hot.

There are two great home traditions. Kashmiri Muslim cooking uses shallots, garlic and a spice cake called ver, and is the source of the wazwan. Kashmiri Pandit cooking, the food of the valley's Hindu community, avoids onion and garlic and leans on asafoetida, dry ginger powder, fennel and yoghurt. Both share many dishes, such as rogan josh and dum aloo, cooked in different ways.

Meals at home are simple: a mound of rice, a bowl of haak or a lentil, and a meat or vegetable dish, eaten with the right hand. Bread belongs to breakfast and teatime rather than lunch and dinner. Hospitality is serious; if you are invited into a home, expect several cups of tea and more food than you can eat, and it is polite to accept at least a little.

sections.heading: The wazwan, course by course
paras: A wazwan is the formal feast cooked for weddings and celebrations by a waza, a master cook from a line of cooks. Traditionally guests sit on the floor in groups of four and share a large copper platter called a trami, heaped with rice and topped with kebabs and meats, while more dishes are served course by course. A full wedding wazwan can run to more than a dozen meat dishes.
You do not need a wedding invitation to taste it. Srinagar restaurants serve wazwan dishes a la carte, and some offer a smaller set trami for two to four people. These are the dishes to know:

At a wedding, the meal is opened with a ritual hand-wash: a server brings a copper jug and basin, the tash-t-nari, to each guest. Eat with your right hand, take from the part of the trami in front of you, and leave the gushtaba, the final course, as the sign that the meal is ending.

sections.heading: Nun chai, kahwa and the kandur
paras: Kashmir drinks two teas, and neither is the milky sweet chai of the plains. Nun chai, also called sheer chai, is a pink salt tea. Green tea leaves are boiled long with a pinch of baking soda, then milk and salt are added, and the tea turns a pale pink. Kashmiris drink it at breakfast and again in the afternoon, often with bread dunked in it.

Kahwa is the guest tea: green tea brewed with saffron, cardamom and cinnamon, poured over crushed almonds and sweetened with sugar or honey. It is traditionally made in a copper samovar, and roadside sellers in Srinagar and the hill stations pour it by the cup.

Breakfast bread comes from the kandur, the neighbourhood baker, who fires a clay oven before dawn. Queue with local families for girda, a round, soft flat bread marked with fingertips; lavasa, thin and crisp; tsot; and the sweeter, layered bakarkhani. Two breads and a cup of nun chai cost under ₹100.

sections.heading: Harissa and other winter food
paras: Harissa is Srinagar's winter breakfast. Mutton is cooked overnight with rice, spices and fat in a deep copper pot over a wood fire until it becomes a smooth paste. Shops in the old city, especially around the Jamia Masjid and Khanyar areas, open before dawn from about November to March and sell out by mid-morning. It comes on a plate with hot mustard oil poured over, a seekh kebab and fresh bread, and costs about ₹250–500 a plate.

Winter is also when you see the stored foods of summer: dried tomatoes, turnips, aubergines and gourds, called hokh syun, and smoked fish. Families cook them with mutton or beans through Chillai Kalan, when fresh vegetables are scarce.

sections.heading: Vegetarian Kashmir
paras: Vegetarians eat well here. Kashmiri Pandit cooking has a full range of dishes without meat, and most restaurants in Srinagar and the hill stations serve them.

Haak is the everyday green: collard greens cooked simply with mustard oil, green chilli and asafoetida, eaten with rice. Nadru, lotus stem harvested from the lakes, is cooked in yoghurt as nadru yakhni or fried in batter as nadru monje, a street snack. Dum aloo, whole small potatoes in a red gravy, and chaman kaliya, paneer in a gravy of milk, turmeric and fennel, are both widely available. Rajma from the hill districts, cooked with rice, is a cheap and filling lunch at any local restaurant.

For snacks, look for nadru monje stalls on the Dal boulevard and in the old city in the evening, and for roasted corn on the meadows in summer. Many hotels in Gulmarg and Pahalgam cook for vegetarian Indian families as a matter of course, so ask for Kashmiri dishes by name if you want them rather than a standard north Indian menu.

sections.heading: Saffron, dry fruit and what to take home
paras: Kashmir saffron grows mainly on the karewa plateaus around Pampore, south of Srinagar, and carries a Geographical Indication tag. The flowers are picked by hand from late October to mid-November. Buy sealed packs with the GI label from known shops or growers' outlets, not loose saffron from roadside sellers. Prices are high, often several hundred rupees a gram.

Walnuts and almonds from Kashmir's orchards, dried apricots, and packs of kahwa mix make good gifts. Shilajit and so-called rare herbs sold to tourists are best avoided. Take sealed food packs in checked luggage, and check airline rules for liquids such as honey.

sections.heading: How to eat well in Srinagar
paras: Ask hotels and houseboats which family-run restaurants they use for wazwan, and go at lunchtime when dishes are freshest. Ahdoos on Residency Road has served Kashmiri food for about a century and is a reliable first stop. In the old city, food is cheaper and more local, but dress modestly and avoid the hour around Friday prayers.

Wazwan dishes are rich. Share plates, order rice by the half, and drink kahwa after the meal, which Kashmiris say helps digestion. During Ramadan many local eateries close by day and open after sunset, while hotel restaurants stay open for guests.

faqs.a: Wazwan is the Kashmiri formal feast cooked by a master cook called a waza, mostly of mutton dishes such as tabakh maaz, rista, rogan josh, yakhni and gushtaba. At weddings guests share a large copper platter, the trami, in groups of four. In Srinagar you can order wazwan dishes a la carte or as a smaller set trami.

faqs.q: How much does a wazwan meal cost in Srinagar?
faqs.a: A single wazwan dish with rice costs about ₹350–650 at a mid-range restaurant. A set trami for four with several dishes costs about ₹2,500–4,500, depending on the place and the number of courses. Simple local restaurants are cheaper; hotel restaurants charge more.

faqs.q: What is nun chai and how does it taste?
faqs.a: Nun chai is Kashmir's pink salt tea: green tea leaves boiled with a pinch of baking soda, then milk and salt are added. It tastes savoury and creamy, more like a light broth than a sweet chai. It is drunk with breakfast breads such as girda and kulcha, and costs ₹20–50 a cup.

faqs.q: What is the difference between kahwa and nun chai?
faqs.a: Kahwa is a clear green tea with saffron, cardamom, cinnamon and crushed almonds, usually sweetened, and served to guests. Nun chai is pink, milky and salted, and drunk daily at breakfast and in the afternoon. Both start with green tea leaves, but the taste and the occasion are completely different.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians eat well in Kashmir?
faqs.a: Yes. Try haak greens with rice, nadru yakhni made with lotus stem in yoghurt, dum aloo, chaman kaliya made with paneer in a milk and turmeric gravy, and rajma with rice. Kashmiri Pandit cooking is a full vegetarian tradition. Most Srinagar restaurants and hotels have vegetarian menus, and bakeries and kahwa sellers are vegetarian by default.

faqs.q: When and where can I eat harissa?
faqs.a: Harissa is sold from about November to March, early in the morning, at old-city shops in Srinagar, especially around the Jamia Masjid and Khanyar. Go between 6 and 9 am, as shops sell out by mid-morning. A plate with mustard oil, a kebab and fresh bread costs about ₹250–500.

faqs.q: How do I buy real Kashmir saffron?
faqs.a: Buy sealed packs carrying the Kashmir saffron GI label from established shops or growers' outlets in Pampore or Srinagar. Real threads are deep red with lighter tips and colour water slowly over several minutes. Avoid loose saffron sold cheaply by roadside sellers. Expect prices of several hundred rupees per gram.

Not usually. The red colour comes from mild Kashmiri chillies and cockscomb flower, not heat. Dishes rely on fennel, dry ginger, cardamom and cinnamon for flavour. Rogan josh and some Pandit dishes can be warm, but most visitors find Kashmiri food richer rather than hotter than north Indian restaurant food.

faqs.q: Are restaurants open during Ramadan in Kashmir?
faqs.a: Many local restaurants and dhabas in Srinagar close during daylight hours in Ramadan and open after sunset for iftar and later meals. Hotel restaurants stay open for guests, and some places serve travellers discreetly. Eat and drink discreetly in public during the day as a courtesy. Bakeries often open before dawn for sehri.
